unit.unitOverview: Conditionals are where English does something that looks illogical until you see the system: it uses a past tense to talk about the present, and a present tense to talk about the future. This unit covers the three you need, in order of distance from reality, plus the one word that catches almost everybody. It ends with an insurance policy, because a policy is nothing but conditions and the whole of it turns on which one you meet.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns and they form a scale.
Open Patterns. Card 3 uses a past tense for something that is not past — read the worked example twice.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is an insurance policy and a rejected claim.
Do the Practice. Practice 4 is where unless goes wrong.
Record yourself using all three conditionals about one situation.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Conditionals have a reputation for difficulty and most of it comes from the numbering. Zero, first, second — those names tell you nothing. So let me give you the actual system, which is a scale of distance from reality.
The further the situation is from being real, the further back the verb goes in time. That is the whole idea, and once you have it, the three forms follow.
Start with the zero conditional, which is not really a conditional at all. It describes something that is always true.
If you heat water to a hundred degrees, it boils. If the alarm sounds, everybody leaves.
Both halves are present simple. If plus present, present. And notice you could replace if with when and nothing changes: when you heat water to a hundred, it boils. That is the test for a zero conditional — if when fits, it is this one.
This is the form of rules, instructions, machines and physical facts. Contracts are full of it.
Second: the first conditional. A real possibility in the future.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel. If you send it today, it will arrive on Monday.
The pattern is: if plus present simple, then will plus the plain verb.
And here is the thing that looks wrong and is not. The if half uses the present tense to talk about the future. If it rains tomorrow — not if it will rain tomorrow. English never puts will after if in this pattern. That is the single most common error with the first conditional, and the rule has no exceptions worth your attention: no will in the if clause.
The first conditional is for things that might genuinely happen. It may rain. You may send it. Nothing about it is imaginary.
Third: the second conditional. Now we move away from reality.
If I had more time, I would finish it. If I won the money, I would leave tomorrow.
The pattern is: if plus past simple, then would plus the plain verb.
And here is the illogical-looking part. That past tense is not about the past at all. If I had more time is about now — I do not have more time, now. The past form is doing something else: it marks distance from reality.
That is why the system is worth seeing as a scale. The further from real, the further back the verb. Present for real, past for unreal. The tense is not measuring time; it is measuring likelihood.
So when do you choose the second rather than the first? When the situation is unlikely, imaginary, or simply not true.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel. It might rain. That is first.
If it rained in the desert, everything would change. It does not. That is second.
And the important one for real conversation: the second conditional is how English gives advice and makes polite suggestions without sounding presumptuous. If I were you, I would ask. That is softer than you should ask, and it is used constantly.
One form note. With be, the second conditional traditionally uses were for every person — if I were you, if he were here. You will also hear was, and it is not wrong in speech. But if I were you is a fixed phrase and it is always were.
Fourth: unless. This is the one that catches people.
Unless means if not.
I will go unless it rains. Same as: I will go if it does not rain.
The error is doubling the negative. Unless it does not rain means if it does not not rain, which is nonsense, and it is extremely common because unless feels like it needs a negative to follow it. It does not. Unless is already negative.
So the rule: after unless, use a positive verb. Unless it rains. Unless you tell me. Unless something changes.
And one thing about meaning that matters in documents. Unless usually means the only thing that would stop it. I will go unless it rains says that rain is the single exception. That is stronger than if not, and it is why insurance policies and contracts use unless so heavily — it closes off everything except the named exception.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The Tense Measures Distance, Not Time
readings.passageScript:
The hardest thing about conditionals is not the forms. It is that English uses a past tense for something that is not past, and until you see why, it looks like an error.
If I had more time, I would finish it.
Had is a past form. The sentence is about now. I do not have more time, at this moment.
So what is the past tense doing? It is not measuring time. It is measuring distance from reality.
That is the system, and it makes all three conditionals one idea rather than three rules.
Something always true — present tense, no distance at all. If you heat water to a hundred, it boils.
Something that might really happen — present tense in the if half, will in the other. If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel. Still real, still close.
Something unlikely or untrue — step back one tense. If it rained in the desert, everything would change.
The further from real, the further back the verb goes. That is all the numbering is trying to say, and it says it badly.
English is not alone in this and it is not arbitrary. Moving a verb backwards to signal unreality is common across languages, and it is the same instinct that makes I was wondering whether you could help more polite than I wonder whether you can — the past form creates distance, and distance is politeness.
Which brings up the most useful thing in this unit. If I were you, I would ask.
That is a second conditional, and it is the standard way English gives advice. It is softer than you should ask because the past form puts distance between the speaker and the instruction. You are not telling somebody what to do; you are describing what you would do in a situation that is explicitly not real, because you are not them.

readings.title: Unless Is Already Negative
readings.passageScript:
Unless means if not. That is the whole definition, and it produces one very common error.
I will go unless it rains.
I will go if it does not rain.
Those are the same sentence. The negative is inside unless, which means you do not add another one.
Unless it does not rain is the error, and it is extremely frequent, because unless feels like a word that ought to be followed by a negative. It is not. After unless, use a positive verb.
Unless it rains. Unless you tell me. Unless something changes. Unless there is a backup.
Now the part that matters in documents, which is about meaning rather than form.
Unless is stronger than if not. It usually signals that the named thing is the only exception.
I will go if it does not rain leaves room for other reasons not to go.
I will go unless it rains says rain is the one thing that would stop me.
This is why contracts, policies and notices use unless so heavily. It closes off everything except the stated exception, and it does so in one word.
You will also meet its relatives. Provided and provided that mean only if, and they are the positive version of the same closing move — you can claim provided you reported it in time. Otherwise means if not and comes after the main clause: report it within 48 hours; otherwise the claim fails.
All four — unless, if not, provided, otherwise — do closely related jobs, and a document will often use several of them in one paragraph. When you read one, the useful question is always the same: what exactly is the exception, and does my situation fall inside it or outside it?
That question is the difference between a claim that is paid and one that is not.

readings.passageScript:
POLICY - SECTION 4: DELAY AND CANCELLATION

  4.1  We will pay up to 300 per person if
       your departure is delayed by more
       than 12 hours, provided the delay
       is confirmed in writing by the
       carrier.

  4.2  We will not pay unless you checked
       in at the time shown on your ticket.

  4.3  If you cancel your trip, we will
       pay your unrecoverable costs only
       if the reason is one listed in 4.4.

  4.4  Listed reasons: illness of the
       insured person; jury service;
       redundancy; damage to your home
       making it uninhabitable.

  4.5  Claims must be submitted within 31
       days. Otherwise they will not be
       considered.

-----------------------------------------

  LETTER REFUSING A CLAIM

  Dear Ms Osei,

  Thank you for your claim of 3 May
  regarding your delayed departure on
  18 April.

  Your flight was delayed by 14 hours,
  which meets the threshold in 4.1, and
  you submitted within 31 days as required
  by 4.5.

  However, the airline has confirmed that
  you were not checked in at the time
  shown on your ticket. Under 4.2 we
  cannot pay unless check-in took place
  at that time.

  We also note that no written
  confirmation of the delay has been
  supplied by the carrier, as 4.1
  requires.

  If you are able to supply written
  confirmation and evidence of check-in,
  we will reconsider.

grammar.title: The zero conditional
grammar.explanation: For things that are always true — rules, machines, physical facts. It is barely a conditional at all, and there is a one-word test for it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IF + PRESENT SIMPLE, PRESENT SIMPLE

  If you heat water to 100, it boils.
  If the alarm sounds, everybody leaves.
  If you press this, the door unlocks.

THE TEST: swap IF for WHEN.
  If nothing changes -> When nothing changes
  Same meaning? -> zero conditional.

  "If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel"
  -> "When it rains tomorrow"? No.
     So that one is NOT zero.

WHERE YOU MEET IT
  instructions, machines, rules,
  physical facts, contracts.

BOTH HALVES ARE PRESENT.
  No will. No would. Nothing else.

EITHER ORDER WORKS
  If the alarm sounds, everybody leaves.
  Everybody leaves if the alarm sounds.
  ^ comma only when IF comes first.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to state what happens when the alarm goes off. It happens every time.
1. Is it always true? Yes — that is a rule, not a possibility.
2. Zero conditional: both halves present simple.
3. If the alarm sounds, everybody leaves.
4. Check with the test: when the alarm sounds, everybody leaves. Same meaning, so it is confirmed.
Now compare something that is not zero. It might rain tomorrow.
1. Apply the test: when it rains tomorrow, we will cancel. That changes the meaning — when says it definitely will rain.
2. So this is not zero. It is a real future possibility, which is card 2.
The test takes two seconds and it separates the first two conditionals cleanly, which is worth having because they look similar on the page.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting will into a zero conditional — if the alarm sounds, everybody will leave. That is not wrong exactly, but it turns a standing rule into a prediction about one occasion. If you mean it always happens, both halves stay present.
grammar.memoryTip: If when fits with no change of meaning, it is the zero conditional.
grammar.practice:
Write the zero conditional, then test it with when.
1. Heat water to a hundred. It boils.
2. The alarm sounds. Everybody leaves.
3. You press this. The door unlocks.
4. The trolley is overloaded. It tips.
5. You do not check in. The claim fails.
6. Now write one that fails the when test, and say why.
grammar.answerKey:
1. If you heat water to a hundred, it boils.
2. If the alarm sounds, everybody leaves.
3. If you press this, the door unlocks.
4. If the trolley is overloaded, it tips.
5. If you do not check in, the claim fails.
6. Model: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel. When it rains tomorrow changes the meaning to a certainty, so it is not zero — it is a real future possibility.
All five of the first group survive the when test unchanged, which is what makes them zero conditionals.
Number 5 is worth noticing: a negative in the if half is fine. It is still always true.

grammar.title: The first conditional
grammar.explanation: For a real possibility in the future. The form contains the single most common conditional error in English, and the rule against it has no exceptions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IF + PRESENT SIMPLE, WILL + PLAIN VERB

  If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel.
  If you send it today, it will arrive
     on Monday.
  If nothing changes, we will finish
     on Friday.

NO WILL AFTER IF. EVER.
  If it will rain tomorrow  <- WRONG
  If it rains tomorrow      <- right

  The present tense in the IF half is
  doing future work. That is normal and
  it is not a mistake.

WHEN TO USE IT
  the thing might genuinely happen.
  Nothing imaginary about it.

OTHER WORDS THAT WORK LIKE IF HERE
  unless, provided, as long as,
  assuming, in case
  -> all take the present, never will.

MAY / MIGHT / CAN instead of WILL
  If it rains, we might cancel.
  ^ same structure, less certain.
grammar.workedExample:
It might rain tomorrow, and if it does you will cancel.
1. Is it a real possibility? Yes — rain tomorrow is entirely possible.
2. So the first conditional: if plus present, then will.
3. The if half: if it rains tomorrow. Present tense, even though it is about the future.
4. The other half: we will cancel.
5. Result: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel.
Now the error to avoid. If it will rain tomorrow, we will cancel. This feels logical — the rain is in the future, so why not will? — and English does not allow it. The if clause carries the future meaning in a present form.
And notice this applies to the whole family: unless it rains, provided it does not rain, as long as it stays dry. All present, never will.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting will after if. It is the commonest conditional error and the one that is most audible, because the sentence sounds doubled — will in both halves. The rule is absolute in this pattern: the if clause takes the present, and the future meaning is carried anyway.
grammar.memoryTip: No will after if. The present tense does the future work.

2. You might send it today. It will arrive Monday.
3. Nothing might change. We will finish Friday.
4. You might not check in. The claim will fail.
5. She might ask. I will explain.
6. Rewrite number 1 using unless.
grammar.answerKey:
1. If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel.
2. If you send it today, it will arrive on Monday.
3. If nothing changes, we will finish on Friday.
4. If you do not check in, the claim will fail.
5. If she asks, I will explain.
6. Unless it rains tomorrow, we will not cancel. (Or, keeping the original meaning: We will go ahead unless it rains.)
No if clause here contains will. Check every one of yours — that is the single thing this card exists to fix.
Number 6 shows the unless family taking the present in exactly the same way.

grammar.title: The second conditional
grammar.explanation: For the unlikely, the imaginary or the untrue. The past tense in it is not about the past — it marks distance from reality.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IF + PAST SIMPLE, WOULD + PLAIN VERB

  If I had more time, I would finish it.
  If I won the money, I would leave.
  If it rained in the desert, everything
     would change.

THE PAST TENSE IS NOT ABOUT THE PAST
  "If I had more time" is about NOW.
  I don't have more time, now.

  The past form marks DISTANCE FROM REAL.
  Further from real -> further back.

FIRST OR SECOND?
  might really happen -> first
     If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel.
  unlikely or untrue -> second
     If it rained in the desert...

ADVICE - the most useful use
  If I were you, I would ask.
  ^ softer than "you should ask"

WERE, NOT WAS
  if I were you, if he were here
  You will hear was in speech and it is
  fine - but "if I were you" is fixed.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say what you would do about time you do not have.
1. Is it true? No — you do not have more time. That is distance from reality.
2. So the second conditional: if plus past simple, then would.
3. If I had more time, I would finish it.
4. Check what the past tense is doing. Not describing the past — marking that the situation is untrue now.
Now the advice use, which is what you will need most.
1. Somebody is unsure whether to ask about something.
2. You are not them, so the situation is explicitly unreal.
3. If I were you, I would ask.
4. Compare you should ask. Yours is softer, because the past form has put distance between you and the instruction.
And the choice against the first conditional: if it rains tomorrow, we will cancel — that might happen. If it rained in the desert, everything would change — it does not.
grammar.commonMistake: Using would in the if clause — if I would have more time. Would belongs in the other half only. The other error is choosing the second conditional for something that might genuinely happen, which quietly tells the listener you think it is unlikely — if it rained tomorrow, we would cancel says you are not expecting rain.
grammar.memoryTip: Past tense for unreal. Would goes in the other half, never after if.
grammar.practice:
Write the second conditional.
1. You do not have more time. You would finish it.
2. You will not win the money. You would leave tomorrow.
3. It does not rain in the desert. Everything would change.
4. There is no alternative. You would take it.
5. You are not them. Give advice: ask.
6. Now write number 1 as a first conditional and say what changes.
grammar.answerKey:
1. If I had more time, I would finish it.
2. If I won the money, I would leave tomorrow.
3. If it rained in the desert, everything would change.
4. If there were an alternative, I would take it.
5. If I were you, I would ask.
6. If I have more time, I will finish it. — this now says there is a real chance of having more time. The second conditional said there is not.
Numbers 4 and 5 both use were: there were an alternative, if I were you. Were is the traditional form for every person here, and if I were you is fixed.
Number 6 is the point of the card. The same two facts, and the tense alone tells the listener how likely you think it is.

grammar.title: Unless
grammar.explanation: Unless means if not. The negative is already inside it, and forgetting that produces the most common error in this area.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
UNLESS = IF NOT

  I will go unless it rains.
  = I will go if it does not rain.

USE A POSITIVE VERB AFTER IT
  unless it rains          right
  unless it does not rain  WRONG
     (= if it does not not rain)

  Unless FEELS like it needs a negative.
  It does not. It already has one.

IT IS STRONGER THAN IF NOT
  "if it does not rain" leaves room for
     other reasons not to go.
  "unless it rains" says rain is the
     ONLY thing that would stop me.

  This is why contracts use it so much:
  one word closes off everything except
  the named exception.

THE FAMILY
  unless      = if not
  provided    = only if
  otherwise   = if not (comes after)
  only if     = and no other reason

READING QUESTION, ALWAYS:
  what exactly is the exception, and am I
  inside it or outside it?
grammar.workedExample:
You intend to go, and rain is the one thing that would stop you.
1. You could say: I will go if it does not rain.
2. Unless is stronger and shorter, because it signals rain is the only exception.
3. Unless takes a positive verb — the negative is already inside it.
4. Result: I will go unless it rains.
5. Check the error: unless it does not rain would mean if it does not not rain, which is nonsense.
Now read one in a document. A policy says: we will not pay unless you checked in at the time shown on your ticket.
1. What is the exception? Checking in on time.
2. Am I inside it or outside it? If you did not check in on time, you are outside, and unless makes it absolute — there is no other route to payment.
That second step is the whole practical skill, and it is the difference between a claim paid and one refused.
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling the negative — unless it does not rain, unless you do not tell me. Extremely common, and it happens because unless feels like a negative word that wants a negative after it. It is a negative word, which is exactly why it does not. The other error is treating unless as identical to if not in a document, when unless usually names the sole exception.
grammar.memoryTip: Unless is already negative. Use a positive verb after it.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each with unless.
1. I will go if it does not rain.
2. The claim fails if you do not report it in time.
3. We will finish on Friday if nothing changes.
4. They will not know if you do not tell them.
5. Nothing will be arranged if you do not commit.
6. One failure stops everything if there is no backup.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I will go unless it rains.
2. The claim fails unless you report it in time.
3. We will finish on Friday unless something changes.
4. They will not know unless you tell them.
5. Nothing will be arranged unless you commit.
6. One failure stops everything unless there is a backup.
Every verb after unless is positive — rains, report, changes, tell, commit, there is. If any of yours has a negative in it, that is the doubling error.
Numbers 3 and 6 are worth checking: nothing changes became something changes, and there is no backup became there is a backup. The negative moved out of the verb and into unless.

writing.promptAndInstructions:

writing.modelText:
If a delivery arrives after four, it is not processed until the next morning. If the driver has no signature, the item goes back to the depot. If it goes back twice, the customer is charged.

activities.instructionsAndItems:
Complete each sentence. No will in the if clause.
1. If it ____ (rain) tomorrow, we ____ (cancel).
2. If you ____ (send) it today, it ____ (arrive) on Monday.
3. If nothing ____ (change), we ____ (finish) on Friday.
4. If you ____ (not check in), the claim ____ (fail).
5. If she ____ (ask), I ____ (explain).
6. Unless it ____ (rain), we ____ (go ahead).
7. Provided you ____ (tell) them, it ____ (be) fine.
8. If the part ____ (arrive), the engineer ____ (come) on Thursday.
9. As long as nothing ____ (go) wrong, it ____ (be) finished by six.
10. If you ____ (commit) now, we ____ (arrange) it this week.
11. In case it ____ (be) delayed, I ____ (take) an earlier train.
12. If we ____ (not have) a backup, one failure ____ (stop) everything.

1. rains / will cancel  2. send / will arrive  3. changes / will finish  4. do not check in / will fail  5. asks / will explain  6. rains / will go ahead  7. tell / will be  8. arrives / will come  9. goes / will be  10. commit / will arrange  11. is / will take  12. do not have / will stop
No if clause here contains will, and neither do the unless, provided, as long as or in case clauses. That family all behaves identically.
Numbers 4 and 12 have negatives in the if half, which is fine — a negative is not the same as a will.
Number 6 shows unless taking a positive verb, which is card 4.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find the conditions
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find one real document that sets conditions — an insurance policy, a returns policy, terms of entry, a warranty, a deadline notice.
Copy out four conditional clauses exactly.
For each, write down the connector used — if, unless, provided, only if, otherwise — and what exactly the exception is.
Then write one line saying which condition you would be most likely to fail without noticing.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your document.
What most people find: unless and only if do the heavy work, and they appear precisely where the document is protecting itself. The generous-sounding clauses use if; the restrictive ones use unless and only if.
The second finding is the one worth having. The condition people are most likely to fail is almost never the main one. It is a procedural requirement buried in a subordinate clause — keep the receipt, include the reference number, notify within 48 hours, get it in writing. Those cost nothing at the time and are impossible to fix afterwards, which is exactly why they are written as absolute conditions.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Advice from a stranger
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, listen for the second conditional in real speech, especially in advice.
Write down four examples exactly as you heard them.
Note how many used if I were you or if I was you.
Then note whether anybody used you should instead, and how it landed.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: if I were you appears constantly and both were and was are heard, with was common in speech and were more usual in writing. Neither will cause you a problem.
The second finding is about softening. The second conditional appears wherever somebody wants to advise without instructing — I would probably ask first, I would leave it a day, if it were me I would not. All of those are doing the same job, and none of them is grammatically necessary. The past tense is buying distance, and distance is politeness.
You will also notice you should is used, and it is used with people the speaker knows well or has authority over. The choice between the two is about the relationship rather than about the advice.
